tips: Read it as a sermon to believers tempted to give up. The writer calls it "the word of exhortation" (Hebrews 13:22), and its warnings (such as Hebrews 2:1–4; 6:4–8; 10:26–31) are meant to keep readers from drifting away.
Follow the key word "better." Jesus is better than the angels, than Moses, and than the priests, and he brings a better covenant with better promises (Hebrews 1:4; 3:3; 8:6).
Keep Leviticus and Exodus close at hand. The argument depends on the tabernacle, the priesthood, and the Day of Atonement, which Hebrews explains as shadows of Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1).

looksBack.title: Melchizedek
looksBack.text: The mysterious priest-king who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20) and Psalm 110:4 are the basis for calling Jesus a priest "after the order of Melchisedec" (Hebrews 5:6; 7:1–17).

looksBack.title: The heroes of faith
looksBack.text: Hebrews 11 surveys the Old Testament from Abel to the prophets, showing how each one lived by faith.

looksAhead.title: The city to come
looksAhead.text: Abraham "looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:10; 13:14), the city John sees in Revelation 21:2, 10.

tips: Read it like Proverbs for the church. It moves quickly from topic to topic—trials, wisdom, the tongue, wealth, patience—with short, vivid commands.
Listen for echoes of Jesus' teaching, especially the Sermon on the Mount. Compare James 5:12 with Matthew 5:34–37 and James 1:22 with Matthew 7:24–27.
Read James 2:14–26 alongside Paul. James is not denying salvation by faith; he is insisting that real faith shows itself in action: "faith without works is dead" (James 2:26).

looksBack.title: Abraham and Rahab
looksBack.text: James uses Abraham's offering of Isaac (Genesis 22; James 2:21–23) and Rahab's protection of the spies (Joshua 2; James 2:25) as examples of faith at work.

looksBack.title: Elijah's prayer
looksBack.text: James points to Elijah praying for drought and rain (1 Kings 17:1; 18:41–45) as proof that "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much" (James 5:16–18).

looksAhead.title: Faith and works in Paul
looksAhead.text: Paul also teaches that faith is shown in love and good works (Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8–10), so the two letters complement each other.

tips: Read it as a letter to suffering believers. Peter calls his readers "strangers" scattered across Asia Minor (1 Peter 1:1), and he prepares them for "the fiery trial" (1 Peter 4:12).
Notice how Peter grounds every instruction in Christ's example—especially his suffering without retaliation (1 Peter 2:21–24).
Watch how Peter applies Israel's titles to the church: "a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9; Exodus 19:5–6).

looksBack.title: The suffering servant
looksBack.text: Peter draws on Isaiah 53 for his picture of Christ: "by whose stripes ye were healed" (1 Peter 2:24).

looksBack.title: Peter's own failure
looksBack.text: Peter's call to "Feed the flock of God" (1 Peter 5:2) recalls Jesus restoring him after his denials with the words "Feed my sheep" (John 21:15–17).

looksAhead.title: 2 Peter
looksAhead.text: Peter's second letter is written to the same readers (2 Peter 3:1) and turns from suffering to false teaching.

tips: Read it as Peter's last testament. He knows his death is near (2 Peter 1:14) and writes so that his readers will remember the truth after he is gone.
Notice the threat the letter answers: false teachers who deny Christ's return and live immorally (2 Peter 2:1–3; 3:3–4).
Read chapter 3 for its answer to the question of why Christ has not yet returned: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise… but is longsuffering to us-ward" (2 Peter 3:9).

looksBack.title: The transfiguration
looksBack.text: Peter recalls being with Jesus "in the holy mount" and hearing God's voice (2 Peter 1:16–18; Matthew 17:1–5).

looksBack.title: Jude
looksBack.text: Much of 2 Peter 2 closely parallels Jude 1:4–18, using similar examples of judgment against false teachers.

looksAhead.title: New heavens and a new earth
looksAhead.text: Peter looks for "new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness" (2 Peter 3:13), which John sees in Revelation 21:1.

tips: Read it as a letter of assurance. John writes "that ye may know that ye have eternal life" (1 John 5:13), giving tests of genuine faith.
Watch for the three tests that keep returning: believing that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh, obeying God's commands, and loving one another.
Understand the background. Some people had left the church teaching that Jesus had not truly come in the flesh (1 John 2:19; 4:2–3), and those who remained were shaken.

looksBack.title: John's Gospel
looksBack.text: The letter's opening (1 John 1:1–3) echoes John 1:1–14, and its call to love one another repeats Jesus' new commandment (John 13:34; 1 John 3:11).

looksBack.title: Cain and Abel
looksBack.text: John points to Cain, who killed his brother (Genesis 4:8; 1 John 3:12), as the opposite of love.

looksAhead.title: 2 and 3 John
looksAhead.text: The two short letters that follow apply the same concerns—truth and love—to particular churches and leaders.

tips: Read it alongside 1 John. In just thirteen verses, the elder applies the same two themes—walking in truth and loving one another—to a specific church.
Notice the practical warning: do not welcome travelling teachers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (2 John 1:7–10).
Read "the elect lady and her children" (2 John 1:1) as most likely a church and its members, which explains the greetings from "thy elect sister" (2 John 1:13).

looksBack.title: The commandment from the beginning
looksBack.text: The elder reminds the church of the commandment "which we had from the beginning, that we love one another" (2 John 1:5; 1 John 2:7; John 13:34).

looksAhead.title: 3 John
looksAhead.text: 3 John deals with the other side of the same issue: welcoming faithful travelling teachers (3 John 1:5–8).

tips: Read it as a personal note with three characters: Gaius, who is praised for his hospitality; Diotrephes, who "loveth to have the preeminence" (3 John 1:9); and Demetrius, who is commended (3 John 1:12).
Notice the practical concern. Travelling missionaries depended on believers to house and support them, and Diotrephes was refusing to receive them.
Take its lesson simply: "follow not that which is evil, but that which is good" (3 John 1:11).

looksBack.title: Hospitality
looksBack.text: Supporting travelling teachers continues the practice Jesus commanded when he sent out his disciples (Matthew 10:9–13).

looksAhead.title: 2 John
looksAhead.text: Together with 2 John, the letter shows both sides of hospitality: welcome those who bring the truth, and refuse those who deny it (2 John 1:10).

tips: Notice the change of plan in Jude 1:3. Jude intended to write about salvation but instead urges his readers to "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."
Watch for Jude's groups of three: three examples of judgment (Jude 1:5–7), three Old Testament rebels—Cain, Balaam, and Korah (Jude 1:11)—and many other triplets.
Don't miss the ending (Jude 1:24–25). After a letter full of warnings, Jude closes with praise to God, who "is able to keep you from falling."

looksBack.title: Old Testament examples
looksBack.text: Jude draws on the exodus generation (Numbers 14), Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19), Cain (Genesis 4), Balaam (Numbers 22–24), and Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16).

looksAhead.title: 2 Peter
looksAhead.text: Much of Jude is closely paralleled in 2 Peter 2, which uses similar language about false teachers.

tips: Read it as three kinds of writing at once: a letter to seven real churches (chapters 2–3), a prophecy, and an apocalypse—a vision that uses symbols to reveal what is really happening behind history.

Look up the Old Testament background. Revelation alludes to the Old Testament constantly, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Exodus; many of its images (lampstands, beasts, plagues, the river of life) appear there first.

Keep the main message in view: the Lamb who was slain has conquered, and God will make all things new (Revelation 5:5–6; 21:5). Christians interpret the details in different ways, but all share that hope.

looksBack.title: Eden restored
looksBack.text: The tree of life and the river of Eden (Genesis 2:9–10) return in the Bible's final chapter, and "there shall be no more curse" (Revelation 22:1–3; Genesis 3:17).

looksBack.title: The plagues of Egypt
looksBack.text: The trumpets and bowls of judgment (Revelation 8; 16) echo the plagues on Egypt in Exodus 7–11, and the redeemed sing "the song of Moses" (Revelation 15:3).

looksAhead.title: The end of the story
looksAhead.text: As the final book, Revelation completes the story begun in Genesis: God dwelling with his people in a new creation (Revelation 21:3).
